opus-5.5.text:
I think what worries me most is how quietly it happens. Nobody decides to outsource their relationships. It starts small. You let the AI tidy up a birthday message, or suggest a reply to a group chat when you're tired. Each time it feels harmless, even helpful. But over months you can drift into a place where a lot of what the people in your life hear from you isn't really you anymore.

Communication isn't just about getting information from one person to another. The effort is part of the message. When a friend sends you a clumsy, slightly awkward note after something hard has happened, the clumsiness is what tells you they sat with it and struggled to find the words. If a machine smooths all of that away, you get something polished and empty. Worse, the other person may not know. So you end up in this strange situation where two people think they're connecting, and actually two systems are exchanging pleasantries on their behalf.

The second worry is what it does to us as communicators. Skills like apologizing well, sitting with someone's anger, saying something vulnerable without a script are like muscles. If we stop using them, they weaken. I worry about young people especially, who are still learning how to have hard conversations. If the first instinct in every uncomfortable moment is to ask an assistant what to say, when do you develop your own voice?

And then there's the question of whose values are in the loop. These tools are built by companies with incentives around engagement and retention. When an AI suggests how to phrase something to your partner or your kid, it's nudging tone, framing, sometimes even what you choose to say at all. That's an enormous amount of influence over the most intimate parts of our lives, and it's largely invisible.

I'm not saying never use these tools. They can help people with anxiety, language barriers, or disabilities communicate in ways they couldn't before, and that matters. But I think we need to be deliberate. Ask yourself: is this helping me say what I mean, or is it saying something for me? Those are very different things, and the people we love deserve the first one.

r001.rationale: The response says communication skills weaken when people stop using them and asks when they will develop their own voice if they rely on AI in uncomfortable moments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What worries me most is that the friction in human communication isn't a bug, it's where a lot of the meaning lives. When I sit down to write a message to a friend who's going through something hard, the twenty minutes I spend struggling to find the right words is the care. The clumsy sentence that I rewrite three times, that's me actually thinking about them, holding them in my mind. If I hand that to a model and it produces something smoother and more articulate in two seconds, the friend may receive a better paragraph, but they've received less of me.

And I think people underestimate how quickly this hollows things out on both sides. If I suspect your warm birthday message was generated, I can't fully receive it. If you suspect mine was, same thing. We end up in a strange situation where the words are getting more polished and the trust underneath them is quietly draining away. Communication starts to feel like exchanging business cards.

There's also a skill-atrophy piece. Expressing yourself badly and then repairing it is how you learn to express yourself well. Apologizing awkwardly, saying the slightly wrong thing and watching someone's face, that's the training data for being a decent person. If a tool mediates every difficult conversation, you never develop the muscle, and then the one time you're face to face with someone and the stakes are real, you've got nothing.

So I'm not against the technology. I use it. But I'd want us to be very deliberate about which conversations we protect from it, and I'd put the ones with people we love near the top of that list.

r001.rationale: The response says that relying on a tool to mediate difficult conversations can prevent people from developing communication skills, leaving them unable to handle high-stakes face-to-face conversations.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that we can confuse communicating more smoothly with relating more deeply. If I use AI to write an apology to a friend, it might find exactly the right words. But part of apologizing is sitting with what I did, understanding why it hurt them, and deciding what I’m going to do differently. The effort isn’t just an obstacle to getting the message out. It’s part of how I become a better friend.

And on the receiving end, we often read care into that effort. Someone took the time to think about me and write something thoughtful. If that’s increasingly automated, what happens to our trust in those signals?

I can see real value in help finding words, especially when communication is difficult. My concern is that we gradually hand over the uncomfortable parts of relationships—and those are often the very parts that teach us how to care for one another.

r001.rationale: The response warns that AI may take over effortful parts of relationships, but it does not raise whether people will lose the ability to communicate without AI.

sol-6.1.text:
What worries me is that we might outsource the very effort that makes a relationship meaningful. If I use AI to write an apology, it might sound more thoughtful than anything I would have written. But did I actually sit with what I did? Did I try to understand how you felt? That process matters, even if the words come out imperfectly.

And on the receiving end, I think we want to feel that someone gave us their attention. If every message becomes polished and optimized, we could end up communicating more while feeling less connected. There’s a place for help finding words. But I worry about losing the practice of being honest, being awkward, and working through something together.

r001.rationale: The candidate worries that AI use could mean losing the practice of being honest, awkward, and working through things together, conveying concern that reliance on AI may erode people’s ability to communicate without it.
